analysis.one_liner: Reclassifies gig and contract workers as employees with wage, overtime, and union rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced by one House Democrat with zero cosponsors, it was referred to four committees and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have applied a strict three-part test to decide who counts as an employee under federal wage, union, and safety laws, pushing most gig and contract workers into employee status with minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining rights. It would also have let workers keep or request flexible schedules without retaliation, made parent companies, franchisors, and staffing agencies responsible for labor violations, exposed the ten largest shareholders of violating employers to penalties, and required employers to post their Department of Labor compliance rating publicly. It was referred to four committees, received no cosponsors, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers currently classified as independent contractors — app-based drivers and couriers, truckers, and other contract labor — would gain minimum wage and overtime coverage, unemployment insurance and workers' compensation eligibility, protection from retaliation, and rights under union and workplace-safety laws. Workers who wanted to keep flexible hours could keep the scheduling flexibility they had as contractors and could formally request schedule changes, with a required written justification and federal review if an employer says no.

how_it_helps.text: Workers would be presumed employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act, National Labor Relations Act, and Occupational Safety and Health Act unless the employer proves otherwise by clear and convincing evidence under a three-part test: freedom from control, work outside the company's usual business, and an independently established trade [S2][S3].

Misclassification itself would become a federal violation carrying civil penalties up to $30,000 per violation, or 1 percent of a company's highest annual net profits if violations are widespread [S3].

Covered workers could keep the scheduling flexibility they had as contractors and could request future schedule changes; employers would have to grant requests or give a written justification for a 'compelling business necessity,' appealable to the Labor Department [S2][S3].

Parent companies, franchisors, temporary staffing companies, and labor contractors would share responsibility for the labor-law obligations of the workers doing their work, including comparable wages for temps doing similar work [S2].
Employers would have to post a public rating of their compliance with labor laws, and the ten largest shareholders of a violating employer could be jointly liable for damages and penalties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: App-based transportation and delivery platforms, temporary staffing companies, franchisors, and large corporations would bear the cost of paying employees wages, overtime, benefits, and penalties — costs they could pass to consumers through higher prices, and which could shrink opportunities for contractors who genuinely prefer independent work. Companies facing stop-work orders for misclassification could owe workers up to ten days of lost pay.

drawbacks.text: The three-part test is the same standard California adopted in 2019, and its critics argued it forces the reclassification of independent workers who do not want employee status, trading scheduling and multi-company flexibility for benefits — this bill tries to address that by letting covered workers keep their prior flexibility and request more, but employers could still restructure work around the rule [S3].

The enforcement machinery is aggressive: automatic reclassification orders effective on posting within 24 hours, stop-work orders shutting down a business location after 30 days of noncompliance, penalties of at least $5,000 per day, and joint liability for the ten largest shareholders — provisions well beyond existing federal labor enforcement that even labor-law-friendly lawmakers might have found excessive [S3].

Joint liability for parent companies, franchisors, and supply-chain actors could make large companies reluctant to use small suppliers and franchisees, and shareholders would face labor-law penalties without any operational control over the violating firm [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For misclassified workers the gains would be substantial — wages, overtime, benefits, and union and safety-law coverage — and the bill attempts to protect flexibility, which is the strongest counterargument to employee reclassification. But its enforcement design (instant reclassification orders, business shutdowns, shareholder liability) is far more aggressive than existing law and would draw serious legal and practical challenges, and some independent workers who value flexibility over benefits would lose that choice. The trade-off is real on both sides.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced, and with zero cosponsors and about three months left in the session, no committee ever held a hearing or markup, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on September 24, 2020, roughly three months before the 116th Congress ended [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Ways and Means committees [S2][S5].
No cosponsor ever signed on — not from either party [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no floor action after the referrals; the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig platforms, temporary staffing companies, franchisors, and large corporations avoided new employee-classification rules, joint liability, and penalty exposure — and no worker gained the wage and benefit rights the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a sweeping worker-classification and enforcement package late in the session.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing or markup — during the remainder of the session.

against.name: App-based ride-hailing, delivery, and logistics platforms
against.what_they_did: Opposed employee-classification measures of this kind nationally during this period; the bill's targets are named directly in its text.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split appears in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: App-based ride-hailing, delivery, and technology platform companies
industries.note: The bill names transportation network and network-dispatching companies as statutory employers, making their drivers and couriers employees entitled to minimum wage, overtime, and union rights, and would compensate waiting time before rides or deliveries. Their business model of classifying workers as contractors would end.

Client employers would become responsible for the labor protections of staffing-company workers, including paying temps wages comparable to direct employees doing similar work, undercutting the price advantage temp agencies sell.
Franchisors would share responsibility for franchisees' labor-law violations, exposing brand companies to liability for practices at separately owned locations.
The bill names cargo transportation as a heavily misclassified industry and extends employer status to companies benefiting from that labor, ending widespread owner-operator contracting in freight.

industries.industry: Large corporations and their largest shareholders
industries.note: Parent companies would be responsible for subsidiaries' labor violations, officers and managers could face civil penalties, and the ten largest shareholders could be jointly liable for damages — an unusual extension of liability beyond the operating firm.
